

# “After accounting for the dependence among multiple effect sizes from the same study, does dialogic reading produce larger effects than non-dialogic reading on the measured outcomes?”

-> This question compares the effect sizes of dialogic and non-dialogic reading after accounting for dependence among multiple effect sizes from the same study.
 

Difference between dialogic and non-dialogic reading
- Y: The intervention used dialogic reading techniques
- N: The intervention did not use dialogic reading techniques
-> the main comparison should be understood as the effect difference between dialogic and non-dialogic reading.


The dataset contians 316 effect sizes extracted from 54 studies 

There can be multiple rows within the same study_id 
= Same children in a study may be measured on multiple outcomes or at post-test and follow-up, so the rows cannot automatically be treated as independent. 


vi is the sampling variance of each yi and is used to account for effect-size precision.

study_id identifies multiple effect sizes from the same study and is used to define study-level clusters.
measure indicates which outcome was measured for each effect size.




```{r}
library(lme4)
library(pbkrtest)
library(RLRsim)
library(ggplot2)
```



```{r}
read <- read.csv(r"(C:\Users\hidy0\Desktop\consultation\reading.csv)")
```


```{r}
head(read)
dim(read)
str(read)
```

So, the main question here is whether dialogic reading produces better results than non-dialogic reading.

The dataset has 316 effect sizes from 54 different studies.

And one important thing is that some studies have multiple effect sizes, so those results aren't necessarily independent.

That's something I needed to account for in the analysis.




#Quality check 

" And then, for the quality check…”

```{r}
colSums(is.na(read))
```
There were some missing values in age, experimenter, and duration, but none in the main variables I needed for the analysis. So I'm not going to deal with those for now.


```{r}

table(read$follow_up, useNA = "ifany")
```
And next, I looked at how the effect sizes were distributed between dialogic and non-dialogic reading.

There were 179 observations for non-dialogic reading and 137 for dialogic reading, so the groups were fairly balanced. That doesn't seem to be a big issue.

And for follow-up, there were only 48 observations, so I think that's something I should take a closer look at later.




```{r} 
as.numeric(table(read$study_id))
```
And I also checked how many effect sizes came from each study.

Some studies had just one, while one had as many as 42.

So, the effect sizes aren't necessarily independent, since some of them come from the same study. 




```{r}
ggplot(read, aes(x = factor(study_id), y = yi)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) + 
  ylim(-2, 9)
```
And I just wanted to see what the effect sizes from the same study actually look like.

It looks like the effect sizes vary across studies, and there are some extreme values, especially in study 22.

So I thought it would make sense to include a random intercept for each study.




```{r}
range(read$yi)
range(read$vi)

summary(read$yi)
summary(read$vi)
```
And then check the range of y and v, just to see if there were any unusual values.

(*The mean being larger than the median suggests that some large positive effect sizes may also be present and that the distribution may not be symmetric.
--> Neither yi nor vi appears perfectly symmetric.

*The minimum vi is 0.025, so all vi values are greater than 0 and there are no invalid variance values.

*range(read$vi) gives 0.025 to 30.9: vi shows how imprecise yi is, so the precision of the most and least precise yi differs by more than 1,000 times. yi values with such different precision shouldn’t be treated equally in the model, so we use weights = 1/vi to give more weight to precise yi) 


And v tells us how much uncertainty there is in y, which is the effect size.

So I'm going to use 1 over v as the weight, to give more weight to the more precise estimates.

And here... v actually varies quite a bit across the data,so giving different weights is even more important.

```{r}

table(read$measure, read$dialogic_reading)
```
(This suggests that measure should be considered together with the main predictor, dialogic_reading, rather than interpreted as a simple separate group comparison.
예를 들어 특정 언어 측정치에 Y 사례가 훨씬 많다면, 전체 Y 결과가 그 측정치의 특성을 많이 반영할 수 있어.
For example, if one language measure contains many more Y cases, the overall Y result may largely reflect that measure’s characteristics)



```{r}
#study conditions
table(read$age, read$dialogic_reading, useNA = "ifany")
table(read$ses, read$dialogic_reading, useNA = "ifany")
table(read$experimenter, read$dialogic_reading, useNA = "ifany")

summary(read$duration)
table(read$duration, useNA = "ifany")
```
And these are the study conditions, like age, SES, experimenter, duration.
And... the two groups are not really balanced, so I'll need to account for these differences in the model.

(The Y and N groups are not fully balanced across study conditions, so differences in yi should not be interpreted as the effect of dialogic reading alone.

ex) N 연구는 교사가 진행한 경우가 많고, Y 연구는 부모가 진행한 경우가 많아요.
N studies were mostly run by teachers, and Y studies mostly by parents.

만약 교사가 진행하면 원래 effect가 더 크게 나온다고 해봐요. 그러면 N 연구의 effect가 커 보이는 건 **”non-dialogic이라서"가 아니라 "교사가 진행해서"**일 수 있어요.
Suppose interventions run by teachers naturally show larger effects. Then N studies might look larger not because they’re non-dialogic, but because teachers ran them.

즉 지금 Y와 N을 비교한 결과에는 dialogic 여부와 진행자 차이가 섞여 있어요. 둘을 구분할 수 없어요.
So the current Y vs. N comparison mixes together the dialogic effect and the difference in who ran it. The two can’t be told apart.

=> The fix: put the conditions in the model)



*Quality Check Summary

1. Effect sizes come from the same study
:Random intercept (1 | study_id)

2. Effect sizes have different levels of uncertainty

$$
w_i = \frac{1}{v_i}
$$



"So, based on the quality check, there are two things I need to consider.

First, some effect sizes come from the same study, so I'm going to use a random intercept for each study.

And second, the effect sizes have different levels of uncertainty, so I'll use 1 over v as the weight." 

(1. If several effect sizes come from the same study, those rows share the study context and may not be independent.
(1 | study_id) allows each study to have its own baseline level. Because the model handles both the average predictor relationship and study-level differences, it uses lmer().

예를 들어 어떤 연구는 전체적으로 효과크기가 높고, 다른 연구는 전체적으로 낮을 수 있어.
For example, one study may generally produce larger effect sizes, while another may produce smaller ones.

이 연구별 차이를 고려한 뒤 dialogic_reading의 관계를 추정하는 거야.
The model estimates the relationship with dialogic_reading after accounting for these study-level differences.


2. y with small v is precise, and y with large v is imprecise.
So before comparing Y and N, we first need to build a model that reflects both points.

*왜 weights = 1/vi를 쓰는가

모델이 예측한 값과 실제 y의 차이가 오차(residual)입니다.
The residual is the difference between the observed y and the model's predicted value.
$$
e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i
$$

그런데 모든 오차를 똑같이 취급하지 않습니다.
v가 작은 y는 더 정밀하게 추정되었으므로, 그 관측값에서 발생한 오차에 더 큰 가중치를 줍니다.
But we do not treat all errors equally. A smaller v means a more precise estimate, so its residual receives greater weight.
Larger v → smaller contribution to the weighted error.

And this formula is part of how the model estimates beta, but it is not the whole calculation.
$$
\sum_i
\frac{
\left(yi_i-\widehat{yi}_i\right)^2
}{
vi_i
}
$$
)


#Model Fitting
 
Now im gonna use Linear Mixed-Effects Regression Model.

because I want to compare Y and N, but I also need to account for differences between studies.

And I'll fit two models. One allows Y and N to have different effects, and the other assumes they have the same effect.

Then I'll compare them to see if there's a real difference.

(*lmer
Linear Mixed-Effects Regression Model
1. Fixed effect: Dialogic reading과 non-dialogic reading의 평균 효과크기 차이
- The average effect-size difference between Y and N.
2. Random effect: 연구마다 서로 다른 기본 효과크기 수준
- Different baseline effect-size levels across studies.) 


Linear Mixed-Effects Regression Model
```{r}
m1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

m0 <- lmer(yi ~ 1 + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

summary(m1)
summary(m0)
``` 

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{dialogic reading}) + \text{study effect} + \text{error}
$$


$$
y = \beta_0 + \text{study effect} + \text{error}
$$

m1: This model estimates the average difference in yi between Y and N.

Fixed: after accounting for study-level differences, Y is estimated to be 0.08296 higher than N on average.
The N group’s average effect is 0.310, and the Y group’s is 0.310 + 0.083 = 0.393.
Y is 0.083 higher than N, but this difference is smaller than its standard error (0.098), so t = 0.85. It’s a size that could easily arise by chance.

Random: Random effect는 연구마다 기본적인 효과크기 수준이 다를 수 있다는 점을 반영해.
A random effect represents the possibility that studies have different baseline effect levels.

0.1067: 연구마다 효과크기가 얼마나 다른지 나타냄
0.1067: shows how much effect sizes vary across studies

1.2022: 모델이 설명하지 못한 변동의 크기를 나타냄
1.2022: shows the amount of variation the model does not explain



```{r}
#whether Y–N difference is significant
KRmodcomp(m1, m0)

confint(m1, method = "Wald")
```
"And the p-value is about 0.4, which is well above 0.05.

The confidence interval also includes zero, so there is no significant difference between Y and N.

So, the simpler model, m0, seems good enough."



(*Kenward-Roger
Null hypothesis: Y and N have the same effect (= m0 is enough)
Alternative hypothesis: Y and N have different effects (= m1 is needed

$$
H_0:\beta_{\text{dialogic}}=0
$$

The Kenward–Roger F-test is designed to test hypotheses about fixed effects.
Kenward–Roger는 F-test를 사용해서 Y와 N의 차이가 통계적으로 유의한지 확인합니다. 이때 mixed model의 구조도 고려해야 합니다.

Kenward–Roger uses an F-test to check whether the difference between Y and N is statistically significant, while accounting for the mixed model.

여기서 자유도가 문제가 됩니다. 우리 데이터는 여러 결과가 같은 연구에서 나왔고, 같은 연구의 결과들은 서로 관련되어 있을 수 있습니다. 그래서 일반 회귀분석처럼 자유도를 간단하게 계산하기 어렵습니다.

The problem here is degrees of freedom. Some results come from the same study, and those results may be related. So we cannot calculate the degrees of freedom as simply as in ordinary regression.

자유도가 적절하지 않으면 p-value도 부정확해질 수 있습니다.

If the degrees of freedom are not appropriate, the p-value may also be inaccurate.

그래서 Kenward–Roger는 모델을 바탕으로 자유도를 추정하고 F-test를 보정합니다. 이를 통해 Y와 N을 구분하는 fixed effect가 통계적으로 유의한지 판단합니다.

So Kenward–Roger uses the model to estimate the degrees of freedom and adjust the F-test. This helps us determine whether the fixed effect for the Y–N difference is statistically significant.

 

(*Two ways to build a confidence interval
The boot method
모델로 가짜 데이터를 만들어요. (PBmodcomp와 같은 방식)
Generate fake data from the model (the same way as PBmodcomp).
가짜 데이터에 모델을 다시 적합해서 “Y − N 차이”를 구해요.
Refit the model to the fake data and get the Y − N difference.
이걸 여러 번 반복해서 차이 값을 많이 모아요.
Repeat many times to collect many difference values.
모은 값들 중 가운데 95%의 범위가 신뢰구간이에요.
The range covering the middle 95% of those values is the confidence interval.

The Wald method
Confidence interval = estimate ± 1.96 × standard error
 
The 95% Wald confidence interval for the effect difference between Y and N runs from −0.109 to 0.275 and includes 0. So the possibility that dialogic and non-dialogic reading have the same effect cannot be ruled out, consistent with the Kenward-Roger test (p = 0.405). Meanwhile, the confidence interval for the N group’s average effect (0.168 to 0.453) excludes 0, so non-dialogic reading also shows an effect greater than 0.)





```{r}
#Model accounting for study conditions
mm1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading+ age + ses + experimenter + duration + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

mm0 <- lmer(yi ~ age + ses + experimenter + duration + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

KRmodcomp(mm1,mm0)
```

"And since Y and N were not evenly distributed across study conditions, 
I also wanted to see if the result would change after accounting for those study conditions."

And the p-value is still above 0.05, around 0.27.

So even after accounting for those study conditions, there is still no significant difference between Y and N.

So, the study conditions do not seem to change the main conclusion.”

 


```{r}
#Test random intercept
set.seed(1) 

m <- lm(yi ~ dialogic_reading, read, weights = 1/vi)

lrt <- 2*(as.numeric(logLik(m1)) - as.numeric(logLik(m, REML = TRUE)))

lrstat <- numeric(1000)

for (i in 1:1000) {
  ry <- unlist(simulate(m))
  null_i <- lm(ry ~ dialogic_reading, read, weights = 1/vi)
  alt_i <- lmer(ry ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)
  lrstat[i] <- 2 * (logLik(alt_i) - logLik(null_i, REML = TRUE))
}

lrt
mean(lrstat > lrt)

```

Result (Full output omitted due to repeated singular fit warnings.)
> lrt
[1] 46.97665
> mean(lrstat > lrt)
[1] 0

"And we also have to test whether we really need the random intercept for each study. And the results suggest that effect sizes from the same study are related, so it makes sense to keep the random intercept."



*lrt represents the improvement in model fit observed in the real data.
 
1. 실제 y에서는 같은 연구의 결과들이 서로 비슷할 수 있지만, 아직 몰라요.
In the real data, results from the same study might be similar, but we do not know yet.

2. 그래서 연구별 공통 효과를 넣지 않은 가짜 데이터 ry를 만들어요.
So we create fake data, ry, without adding a shared effect for each study.

3. 그런데 그런 상황에서 구한 LRT는 모두 실제 LRT보다 작았어요. 즉, 실제 데이터는 가짜 데이터에서 가정한 상황과 다르다는 근거예요.
But all the simulated LRT values were smaller than the real one. So this suggests that the real data do not behave like the simulated data.

4. 따라서 실제 데이터에서는 같은 연구의 결과들이 서로 독립적이지 않다는 것을 뒷받침하고, random intercept를 넣는 것이 타당하다는 결론이에요.
So this supports the idea that results from the same study are not independent, and that including a random intercept makes sense.


*REML (Restricted Maximum Likelihood)
REML은 mixed model에서 연구마다 효과크기가 얼마나 다른지, 즉 random effect의 분산을 더 정확하게 추정하기 위한 방법이에요.
REML helps us estimate how much effect sizes vary between studies, or the random-effect variance, more accurately.
이때 fixed effects를 추정하면서 사용한 정보도 고려해요.
It also accounts for the information used to estimate the fixed effects.
lmer()는 기본적으로 REML을 사용해요.
lmer() uses REML by default. 


logLik: This is called the likelihood. The better the model explains the data, the larger L is.

 
  
```{r}
#Difference between Y and N changes depending on the measure
ma <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading * measure + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)
mb <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + measure + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

KRmodcomp(ma, mb)
```
"And, I wanted to check if the difference between Y and N changes depending on the measure, 
The p-value is about 0.24, so we did not find statistical evidence that the Y–N difference varies by measure."  


$$
y=\beta_0+\beta_1(Y)+\beta_2(\text{measure})+\beta_3(Y\times\text{measure})
\\
Y-N=\beta_1+\beta_3(\text{measure})
$$




#Diagnostic

```{r}
plot(fitted(m1), residuals(m1), xlab ="Fitted", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h=0)

qqnorm(residuals(m1))
qqline(residuals(m1), col = "blue")

ranef(m1)
```

"Now, model diagnostics.

Most residuals are close to zero, but there's one large outlier.

The Q-Q plot also shows some departures from normality and an outlier 

And looking at the random intercepts Study 27 has a much higher value than the other studies."

ranef: How far that study sits above or below the overall level.





```{r}
#10 largest absolute residuals
r <- residuals(m1)

read[order(abs(r), decreasing = TRUE)[1:10], c("es_id", "study_id", "yi", "vi")]
```
"Here are the 10 largest absolute residuals, so we can see which observations stand out the most.
And I'm gonna remove these outliers one by one and see if the Y–N results change." 


(1) Remove 129, 58 es_id
```{r}
read_del1 <- subset(read, !(es_id %in% c(129, 58)))

s1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read_del1, weights = 1/vi)
s0 <- lmer(yi ~ 1 + (1|study_id), read_del1, weights = 1/vi)

summary(s1)
KRmodcomp(s1, s0)

```
"First, I removed effect sizes 129 and 58, but the Y–N difference was still not significant."

"and 27 which we found from the random-intercept analysis, wasn't significant either,"

(2) Remove study_id 27
```{r}
read_del2 <- subset(read, !(es_id %in% c(129, 58)) & study_id != 27)

ss1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read_del2, weights = 1/vi)
ss0 <- lmer(yi ~ 1 + (1|study_id), read_del2, weights = 1/vi)

summary(ss1)
KRmodcomp(ss1, ss0)
```
Study 27, the only study-level extreme identified by ranef, was additionally excluded (310 rows, 53 studies). 


(3) Remove study_id 22 
```{r}
read_del3 <- subset(read, !(es_id %in% c(129, 58)) & !(study_id %in% c(27, 22)))

sss1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read_del3, weights = 1/vi)
sss0 <- lmer(yi ~ 1 + (1|study_id), read_del3, weights = 1/vi)

summary(sss1)
KRmodcomp(sss1, sss0)
```


(4) Remove 297 es_id
```{r}
read_del4 <- subset(read, !(es_id %in% c(129, 58, 297)) & !(study_id %in% c(27, 22)))

t1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read_del4, weights = 1/vi)
t0 <- lmer(yi ~ 1 + (1|study_id), read_del4, weights = 1/vi)

summary(t1)
KRmodcomp(t1, t0)
```
"And for the Study 22 and row 297, the Y–N difference was still not significant. So the conclusion stayed the same."
The results do not provide clear evidence that dialogic reading leads to better outcomes, even after removing the outliers." 

=> The results do not provide clear evidence that dialogic reading leads to better outcomes for children, even after removing the outliers.


결론 
1. p가 다섯 번 모두 0.05보다 커요. 어떤 걸 빼도 “Y와 N의 차이에 근거가 없다”예요.
1. p is above 0.05 in all five. Whatever is removed, the answer is “no evidence of a Y–N difference.”

2. 차이 추정값도 0.08 ~ 0.14 사이에서만 움직여요. 결론이 뒤집힐 만큼 크게 변하지 않았어요.
2. The estimate stays between 0.08 and 0.14. It never moved enough to overturn anything.

3. 그래서 7단계 결론이 이상한 데이터 때문이 아니라는 게 확인됐어요. 이게 8단계의 목적이었어요.
3. So the Step 7 conclusion is confirmed not to be an artifact of the bad data. That was the point of Step 8.




#Follow-up 

N: 개입 직후 (post-test)
N: immediately after the intervention (post-test)
Y: 시간이 지난 뒤 (follow-up)
Y: at a later follow-up

-> Does the effect persist over time?
-> Does the Y–N difference depend on timing?

"And finally, I looked at follow-up to see if the effects changed over time."

```{r}
table(read$dialogic_reading, read$follow_up)

unique(read$study_id[read$follow_up == "Y"])
```
"There isn't enough data to compare Y and N at follow-up, but we can compare the effects right after the program and later on."


N   Y (follow up)
N 140  39
Y 128   9
And Only 9 of the 54 studies measured again later.
= 9=Y vs 39=N → the Y side has only 9 ✗

= 268(Post) vs 48(Follow) 
Both sides have plenty. The comparison works. -> 
질문 1: 효과가 시간이 지나면 약해지는가
Question 1: Do effects weaken over time?



```{r}
m1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

read_f <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading + follow_up + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

summary(read_f)

fixef(m1)["dialogic_readingY"]
fixef(read_f)["dialogic_readingY"]
```
dialogic_readingY 
       0.08295989 
dialogic_readingY 
       0.08298941 
       
```{r}
KRmodcomp(read_f, m1)
```
"So I added follow-up to the model, but the coefficient for the Y–N difference barely changed, And the p-value is 0.91, so adding follow-up didn't really improve the model." 
So basically, the reading program seems to work about the same, even after some time has passed." 


```{r}
read_f1 <- lmer(yi ~ dialogic_reading * follow_up + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)

summary(read_f1)

KRmodcomp(m1, read_f1)
```
read_follow (+)

yi = β₀ + β₁ × Y + β₂ × F + u_study + ε

fA (*)

yi = β₀ + β₁ × Y + β₂ × F + β₃ × (Y × F) + u_study + ε


"There are only 9 follow-up results for Y, but I test the interaction anyway.

The p-value is high and the standard error is large, so as expected, there's no significant difference."



 
<Result>

Main takeaway: No clear evidence that dialogic reading works better than non-dialogic reading.

Conclusion: Pretty consistent across the different analyses.

Based on this dataset: No clear advantage of dialogic reading over non-dialogic reading.

So, the main takeaway is that I didn't find clear evidence that dialogic reading works better than non-dialogic reading.
And the conclusion was pretty consistent across the different analyses.
So, based on this dataset, there doesn't seem to be a clear advantage of dialogic reading over non-dialogic reading.


<Limitation> 

(1) Random effects
Differences between studies considered -> not fully account for differences within each study
Ex) Measure: Vocabulary & Pronunciation might be related closely

-> Original paper: RVE to deal with this issue.

(2) Weights (1/vi)
More weight to more accurate effect sizes 

Caused problems with analysis: some methods didn't handle weights properly

------------------------------
And here are the limitations of my analysis.
My model uses random effects to account for differences between studies, but it doesn't fully account for differences within each study.
For example, some outcomes, like vocabulary and pronunciation, might be related closely , but my model doesn't really capture that.
I also looked at the original paper, and they used RVE to deal with this issue. But that's a method I haven't learned yet.

Another limitation is the weights. I used 1/vi because I wanted to give more weight to more accurate effect sizes.
But this caused some problems with the analysis. For some reason, some methods didn't handle the weights properly, so I couldn't use them.


So yeah, those are the main limitations of my analysis. And that's pretty much it. Thank you! 




내 질문 
PBmodcomp	
confint(method = "boot")
exactRLRT

① PBmodcomp and confint(boot): the fake data are generated wrong
둘 다 모델로 가짜 데이터를 만들어서 쓰는 방법이에요. 그런데 weights가 있는 모델에서 R이 가짜 데이터를 만들면, 원래보다 훨씬 더 크게 흔들리는 데이터가 나와요.
Both generate fake data from the model and work from it. But when R generates fake data from a model with weights, the data come out varying far more than the original.

② exactRLRT: it drops the weights from the comparison model
exactRLRT는 (1|study_id)가 없는 비교 모델을 자기가 만드는데, 그때 weights를 넣지 않아요. 그래서 두 모델이 “study 차이” 말고 “weights 있음/없음”까지 달라져요.
exactRLRT builds the comparison model without (1|study_id) on its own, and leaves the weights out. So the two models differ not only in “study differences” but also in “weights or no weights.”



#Test random intercept
set.seed(1) 

m <- lm(yi ~ dialogic_reading, read, weights = 1/vi)

lrt <- 2*(as.numeric(logLik(m1)) - as.numeric(logLik(m, REML = TRUE)))

lrstat <- numeric(1000)

for (i in 1:1000) {
  ry <- unlist(simulate(m))
  null_i <- lm(ry ~ dialogic_reading, read, weights = 1/vi)
  alt_i <- lmer(ry ~ dialogic_reading + (1|study_id), read, weights = 1/vi)
  lrstat[i] <- 2 * (logLik(alt_i) - logLik(null_i, REML = TRUE))
}

lrt
mean(lrstat > lrt)
